title: Economy & Finance
subtitle: Read the business pages, talk markets and argue about a crisis in confident French

lessons.title: Comprendre l'économie
lessons.description: The core indicators — growth, inflation, unemployment, purchasing power — and how the French press talks about them.

blocks.heading: The four indicators everyone quotes
blocks.body: French economic debate revolves around four figures: "la croissance" (growth of the PIB, the GDP), "l'inflation" (the rise in prices), "le chômage" (unemployment) and "le pouvoir d'achat" (what a salary actually buys). The first three are measured, the fourth is felt — which is why politicians talk about it constantly. Note that French says "la croissance" on its own where English often needs "economic growth".

examples.french: La croissance devrait atteindre 1,2 % cette année.
examples.english: Growth should reach 1.2% this year.
examples.note: French writes decimals with a comma: 1,2 %

examples.french: L'inflation ronge le pouvoir d'achat des ménages.
examples.english: Inflation is eating away at households' purchasing power.

examples.french: Le chômage recule pour le troisième trimestre consécutif.
examples.english: Unemployment is falling for the third quarter in a row.
examples.note: "reculer" = to fall back, the standard verb for a declining indicator

examples.french: Le PIB français a stagné au deuxième trimestre.
examples.english: French GDP stagnated in the second quarter.

examples.french: Les salaires ne suivent pas la hausse des prix.
examples.english: Wages are not keeping up with the rise in prices.

examples.french: On parle de récession après deux trimestres de recul.
examples.english: We speak of a recession after two quarters of decline.

blocks.tip: "Le pouvoir d'achat" is untranslatable politically: it is the single most cited notion in French elections, far more than GDP.

blocks.heading: Supply, demand and prices
blocks.body: The mechanism is described with a small, fixed set of collocations: "l'offre" and "la demande" meet on "le marché"; when "la demande" exceeds "l'offre", "les prix flambent". Verbs are almost always used with "de" for the amount of change: "augmenter de 3 %" means to go up BY 3%, never TO 3%. To say "to", use "passer à" or "atteindre".

examples.french: L'offre ne suffit plus à couvrir la demande.
examples.english: Supply is no longer enough to cover demand.

examples.french: Les prix de l'énergie ont flambé l'hiver dernier.
examples.english: Energy prices soared last winter.
examples.note: "flamber" = to shoot up, very frequent in the press

examples.french: Le prix du billet a augmenté de douze euros.
examples.english: The ticket price went up by twelve euros.

examples.french: Le litre est passé à deux euros.
examples.english: The litre went up to two euros.

examples.french: La consommation des ménages repart doucement.
examples.english: Household consumption is slowly picking up again.

examples.french: Quand la demande faiblit, la production ralentit.
examples.english: When demand weakens, production slows down.

blocks.tip: "Le marché" without a determiner complement means the market in the abstract; "le marché du travail" is the job market, "le marché de l'immobilier" the property market.

blocks.heading: The vocabulary of policy
blocks.body: When the economy stalls, the state has two classic options and French names them clearly: "la relance" (spending to restart activity) and "l'austérité" (cutting to reduce "le déficit" and "la dette publique"). "La Banque centrale" acts on "les taux d'intérêt". These words carry political charge: "austérité" is almost always used critically, while supporters prefer "la rigueur budgétaire".

examples.french: Le gouvernement a lancé un plan de relance de dix milliards.
examples.english: The government launched a ten-billion stimulus plan.

examples.french: La Banque centrale a relevé ses taux d'intérêt.
examples.english: The central bank raised its interest rates.
examples.note: "relever" for rates, not "augmenter"

examples.french: L'austérité a pesé sur les services publics.
examples.english: Austerity weighed on public services.

examples.french: Le déficit s'est creusé de deux points.
examples.english: The deficit widened by two points.
examples.note: "se creuser" = to widen, literally to hollow out

examples.french: La dette publique dépasse les cent pour cent du PIB.
examples.english: Public debt exceeds one hundred percent of GDP.

examples.french: La conjoncture reste incertaine pour les mois à venir.
examples.english: The economic climate remains uncertain for the coming months.

blocks.tip: "Un milliard" is a billion (10⁹) and "un billion" in French is a trillion — a classic false friend in financial reporting.

blocks.heading: Describing variation: de, à, entre
blocks.body: Three prepositions do almost all the work with figures. "De" gives the SIZE of the change (augmenter de 3 %). "À" gives the POINT reached (passer à 2 euros, tomber à 5 %). "Entre… et…" gives a range. Two verbs are worth memorising as a pair: "s'élever à" (to amount to) for totals, and "atteindre" (to reach) for peaks. Never say "augmenter à 3 %" for an increase of 3% — that is the classic English speaker's mistake.

examples.french: Les loyers ont augmenté de 4 % en un an.
examples.english: Rents went up by 4% in a year.

examples.french: Le chômage est tombé à 6,8 %.
examples.english: Unemployment fell to 6.8%.

examples.french: La facture s'élève à trois mille euros.
examples.english: The bill amounts to three thousand euros.

examples.french: L'inflation devrait atteindre son pic en janvier.
examples.english: Inflation should reach its peak in January.

examples.french: La croissance se situe entre 0,5 et 1 %.
examples.english: Growth stands between 0.5 and 1%.

examples.french: Le déficit s'est réduit de moitié.
examples.english: The deficit has halved.
examples.note: "de moitié", "du double", "d'un tiers" all take "de"

blocks.tip: In French, the % sign takes a space before it: "3 %", and decimals use a comma: "1,5 %".

blocks.heading: The journalistic conditional
blocks.body: When French media report a figure they cannot yet confirm, they put the verb in the conditional. "L'inflation atteindrait 4 %" does not mean "would reach" — it means "reportedly reaches / is said to reach". This "conditionnel journalistique" is everywhere in economic reporting, and recognising it is the difference between reading a fact and reading a rumour. In the past, use the conditionnel passé: "aurait perdu".

examples.french: Le groupe supprimerait deux cents postes.
examples.english: The group is reportedly cutting two hundred jobs.

examples.french: La croissance serait plus faible que prévu.
examples.english: Growth is said to be weaker than expected.

examples.french: La banque aurait perdu un milliard en trois jours.
examples.english: The bank reportedly lost a billion in three days.

examples.french: Selon Bercy, le déficit se creuserait encore.
examples.english: According to the Finance Ministry, the deficit would widen further.
examples.note: Bercy = the French finance ministry, by metonymy

examples.french: Les négociations auraient échoué hier soir.
examples.english: The negotiations reportedly failed last night.

examples.french: Il y aurait un accord d'ici la fin du mois.
examples.english: There is said to be a deal coming by the end of the month.

blocks.tip: If a headline uses the conditional, the paper is protecting itself: nothing is confirmed. A confirmed fact goes in the indicative.

items.prompt: Comment on an indicator, out loud.
items.french: Le chômage recule pour le troisième trimestre consécutif.
items.english: Unemployment is falling for the third quarter in a row.
items.tip: "Trimestre" is three clean syllables: tree-MESS-truh, with a barely voiced final -re. Don't stress "con-sé-cu-TIF" until the last syllable.

items.prompt: Say a percentage the French way.
items.french: Les prix ont augmenté de trois virgule cinq pour cent.
items.english: Prices went up by three point five percent.
items.tip: Say "virgule" (veer-GÜL) where English says "point". Round your lips tightly for the ü, as in "tu".

items.prompt: Report an unconfirmed figure using the conditional.
items.french: Selon Bercy, le déficit se creuserait encore l'an prochain.
items.english: According to the Finance Ministry, the deficit would widen further next year.
items.tip: "Creuserait" ends in an open -eh, not -ay: kruh-zuh-REH. That vowel is the whole signal that this is unconfirmed.

passages.title: Les chiffres et le ressenti
passages.french:
Chaque mois, l'INSEE publie ses chiffres, et chaque mois le même malentendu recommence.
L'institut annonce que l'inflation est retombée à deux pour cent ; les ménages, eux, jurent que tout continue d'augmenter.
Les deux ont raison, et c'est précisément ce qui rend le débat si vif.
Un ralentissement de l'inflation ne signifie pas que les prix baissent : il signifie qu'ils montent moins vite qu'avant.
Le paquet de pâtes qui a pris quarante centimes l'an dernier ne les rendra pas cette année.
À cela s'ajoute un décalage bien connu des économistes : nous mémorisons le prix des produits que nous achetons chaque semaine, pas celui des ordinateurs ou des billets d'avion.
Or ce sont justement ces derniers qui tirent l'indice vers le bas.
« Les gens ne se trompent pas, ils mesurent autre chose », résume une chercheuse du CREDOC.
Ce qu'ils mesurent, c'est le pouvoir d'achat : le rapport entre ce qu'ils gagnent et ce que la vie coûte.
Or les salaires, eux, n'ont pas suivi la hausse des prix depuis trois ans.
Le niveau de vie moyen a donc stagné pendant que la croissance, sur le papier, restait positive.
D'où ce sentiment étrange d'une économie qui va bien et d'un porte-monnaie qui va mal.
Le gouvernement promet un plan de relance ; l'opposition réclame une hausse générale des salaires.
Entre les deux, l'économiste hausse les épaules : « Tant que la productivité stagnera, on se disputera le même gâteau. »
passages.english:
Every month, INSEE publishes its figures, and every month the same misunderstanding starts again.
The institute announces that inflation has fallen back to two percent; households, for their part, swear that everything is still going up.
Both are right, and that is precisely what makes the debate so heated.
A slowdown in inflation does not mean that prices are falling: it means they are rising more slowly than before.
The packet of pasta that went up by forty cents last year will not give them back this year.
On top of that comes a lag well known to economists: we memorise the price of the products we buy every week, not that of computers or plane tickets.
Yet it is precisely the latter that pull the index down.
"People are not wrong, they are measuring something else," sums up a researcher at CREDOC.
What they are measuring is purchasing power: the ratio between what they earn and what life costs.
And wages, for their part, have not kept up with the rise in prices for three years.
The average standard of living has therefore stagnated while growth, on paper, remained positive.
Hence that strange feeling of an economy doing well and a wallet doing badly.
The government promises a stimulus plan; the opposition demands a general wage increase.
Between the two, the economist shrugs: "As long as productivity stagnates, we will be fighting over the same cake."

lessons.title: Les marchés
lessons.description: Shares, bonds, returns and risk — the language of the stock market and of talking about your own money.

blocks.heading: La Bourse: the basic pieces
blocks.body: "La Bourse" (capital B for the institution) is where "les actions" (shares) and "les obligations" (bonds) are traded. Beware two false friends: "une action" here is a share, not an action, and "une obligation" is a bond, not a duty. A company listed on the market is "cotée en Bourse", and its share price is "le cours", which "monte", "baisse" or "dévisse".

examples.french: L'entreprise est cotée en Bourse depuis 2019.
examples.english: The company has been listed on the stock exchange since 2019.

examples.french: J'ai acheté vingt actions de ce groupe.
examples.english: I bought twenty shares in that group.

examples.french: Le cours a dévissé de huit pour cent en une séance.
examples.english: The share price plunged by eight percent in a single session.
examples.note: "dévisser" = to plunge; strong, very market-specific

examples.french: Les obligations d'État rapportent peu mais rassurent.
examples.english: Government bonds pay little but they reassure.

examples.french: Le CAC 40 a clôturé en hausse.
examples.english: The CAC 40 closed up.
examples.note: "clôturer en hausse / en baisse" is the fixed phrase

examples.french: Les actionnaires ont voté contre la fusion.
examples.english: The shareholders voted against the merger.

blocks.tip: "Jouer en Bourse" (to play the market) carries a whiff of gambling; a serious investor says "investir en Bourse" or "placer son argent".

blocks.heading: Investing, returns and losses
blocks.body: "Placer" and "investir" are near-synonyms, but "un placement" suggests parking money safely while "un investissement" suggests building something. What the money earns is "le rendement" (yield) or, once you sell, "une plus-value" (capital gain) — the opposite being "une moins-value". "Rentable" describes anything that pays off, from a share to a bakery.

examples.french: J'ai placé mes économies sur un livret.
examples.english: I put my savings into a savings account.

examples.french: Ce placement offre un rendement de trois pour cent.
examples.english: This investment offers a three percent yield.

examples.french: Il a réalisé une belle plus-value à la revente.
examples.english: He made a nice capital gain when he resold.

examples.french: L'opération s'est soldée par une moins-value.
examples.english: The operation ended in a capital loss.
examples.note: "se solder par" = to end in, standard financial phrasing

examples.french: Ce n'est rentable qu'à long terme.
examples.english: It's only profitable in the long term.

examples.french: Il faut diversifier son portefeuille d'actions.
examples.english: You have to diversify your share portfolio.

blocks.tip: The French are famously prudent savers: "le Livret A", a state-guaranteed savings account, holds more money than the whole Paris stock market does from small investors.

blocks.heading: Talking about risk
blocks.body: Risk vocabulary is where finance meets everyday French. "Prendre un risque" is neutral, "prendre des risques inconsidérés" is reckless, and "miser sur" (to bet on) works for shares and for people alike. When markets get nervous, money flows towards "les valeurs refuges" — gold, the Swiss franc — and away from "les valeurs spéculatives".

examples.french: Je préfère un placement sûr à un pari risqué.
examples.english: I prefer a safe investment to a risky bet.

examples.french: Il a tout misé sur les valeurs technologiques.
examples.english: He bet everything on tech stocks.

examples.french: L'or reste la valeur refuge par excellence.
examples.english: Gold remains the ultimate safe haven.

examples.french: La volatilité rend les marchés imprévisibles.
examples.english: Volatility makes markets unpredictable.

examples.french: Les investisseurs prennent leurs bénéfices.
examples.english: Investors are taking their profits.
examples.note: "prendre ses bénéfices" = to cash in, sell at a gain

examples.french: Personne n'a vu venir l'éclatement de la bulle.
examples.english: Nobody saw the bubble bursting coming.

blocks.tip: "Qui ne risque rien n'a rien" — nothing ventured, nothing gained — is the proverb a French broker will quote at you, usually just before you lose money.

blocks.heading: Hypothesis and precaution: si, au cas où, à moins que
blocks.body: Finance talk is full of conditions. "Si" + imparfait announces an unreal or unlikely hypothesis and pairs with the conditionnel: "Si les taux baissaient, j'emprunterais." Two other structures matter at B2: "au cas où" is always followed by the CONDITIONAL (never the subjunctive), and "à moins que" takes the SUBJUNCTIVE, often with the optional "ne explétif". Never write "si j'aurais" — after "si", the conditional is impossible.

examples.french: Si les taux baissaient, j'emprunterais tout de suite.
examples.english: If rates went down, I'd borrow straight away.

examples.french: Au cas où le marché s'effondrerait, gardez des liquidités.
examples.english: In case the market collapses, keep some cash.
examples.note: au cas où + conditionnel, always

examples.french: À moins que la banque ne révise ses taux, je renonce.
examples.english: Unless the bank revises its rates, I'll give up.
examples.note: "ne" here is stylistic, not a negation

examples.french: Si j'avais vendu en mars, j'aurais évité la chute.
examples.english: If I had sold in March, I would have avoided the fall.

examples.french: Je n'investirai pas, à moins d'avoir des garanties.
examples.english: I won't invest, unless I have guarantees.
examples.note: same subject → à moins de + infinitif

examples.french: Au cas où vous auriez un doute, appelez votre courtier.
examples.english: Should you have any doubt, call your broker.

blocks.tip: "Au cas où" can end a sentence on its own, exactly like English "just in case": « Prends ton parapluie, au cas où. »

blocks.heading: Compound relative pronouns: auquel, duquel, dont
blocks.body: Defining financial terms means chaining clauses, and that requires the right relative pronoun. Use "dont" when the verb takes "de" (parler DE quelque chose → le placement dont je parle). Use "auquel / à laquelle / auxquels" when the verb takes "à" (renoncer À → le projet auquel j'ai renoncé). After a preposition other than "de", use "lequel" and its forms. "Duquel" is reserved for complex prepositions like "près de", "à côté de", "au terme de".

passages.title: Rendez-vous chez le conseiller
passages.french:
— Vous avez trente-cinq mille euros qui dorment sur un livret, madame Fournier. C'est prudent, mais l'inflation les grignote.
— Je sais. Seulement, la Bourse, ça me fait peur. Mon père y a laissé des plumes en 2008.
— C'est un souvenir que partagent beaucoup de Français. Mais votre père avait-il diversifié son portefeuille ?
— Franchement, non. Il avait tout misé sur deux valeurs bancaires.
— Voilà exactement le risque dont je voudrais vous protéger. Concentrer, c'est parier ; répartir, c'est investir.
— Et si les marchés dévissent l'an prochain ?
— Alors vous ne vendez pas. Une moins-value n'existe vraiment que le jour où l'on vend.
— Vous me proposez quoi, concrètement ?
— Un fonds diversifié, avec un horizon de huit ans, et un rendement moyen espéré autour de cinq pour cent. Rien n'est garanti, je vous le dis franchement.
— Au moins, vous ne me promettez pas la lune.
— Ce serait malhonnête. En revanche, je vous garantis que laisser dormir votre épargne vous fait perdre du pouvoir d'achat chaque année.
— Autrement dit, ne rien faire est aussi une décision.
— C'est même la plus coûteuse des décisions, à moins que vous n'ayez besoin de cet argent dans deux ans.
— Non. C'est pour la retraite.
— Alors laissez-en dormir dix mille sur le livret, au cas où, et faites travailler le reste.
passages.english:
"You have thirty-five thousand euros sitting idle in a savings account, Mrs Fournier. That's prudent, but inflation is nibbling away at it."
"I know. It's just that the stock market scares me. My father lost a lot there in 2008."
"That's a memory a lot of French people share. But had your father diversified his portfolio?"
"Honestly, no. He'd bet everything on two banking stocks."
"That's exactly the risk I'd like to protect you from. Concentrating is betting; spreading is investing."
"And if the markets plunge next year?"
"Then you don't sell. A capital loss only really exists on the day you sell."
"What are you actually suggesting?"
"A diversified fund, with an eight-year horizon, and an expected average return of around five percent. Nothing is guaranteed, I'll tell you frankly."
"At least you're not promising me the moon."
"That would be dishonest. What I do guarantee, on the other hand, is that letting your savings sleep makes you lose purchasing power every year."
"In other words, doing nothing is also a decision."
"It's even the most expensive of decisions — unless you need this money within two years."
"No. It's for retirement."
"Then leave ten thousand asleep in the savings account, just in case, and put the rest to work."

lessons.title: La crise
lessons.description: Analyse what caused a crisis and what it caused in turn, using the full range of French cause and consequence connectors.

blocks.heading: How a crisis is described
blocks.body: A French account of a crisis follows a predictable arc: something "déclenche" it, it "s'aggrave", the economy "s'effondre", companies "font faillite", and finally there is "une reprise". Two adjectives are essential for the analysis: "conjoncturel" (temporary, tied to the current cycle) versus "structurel" (deep-rooted). Calling a problem "structurel" in French is a serious claim — it means no stimulus plan will fix it.

examples.french: La faillite d'une banque a déclenché la panique.
examples.english: The collapse of one bank triggered the panic.

examples.french: La crise s'est aggravée en quelques semaines.
examples.english: The crisis worsened within a few weeks.

examples.french: Des milliers d'entreprises ont mis la clé sous la porte.
examples.english: Thousands of companies went under.
examples.note: "mettre la clé sous la porte" = to shut up shop

examples.french: Le chômage a explosé chez les jeunes.
examples.english: Unemployment exploded among young people.

examples.french: Ce n'est pas conjoncturel, c'est structurel.
examples.english: This isn't cyclical, it's structural.

examples.french: La reprise s'est amorcée deux ans plus tard.
examples.english: The recovery began two years later.

blocks.tip: "La crise" used alone, with no complement, refers in French conversation to whichever downturn people are living through — 2008, the pandemic, energy prices.

blocks.heading: Naming causes
blocks.body: French has a rich toolbox for cause, and the choice signals your stance. "Parce que" answers a question neutrally. "Car" justifies what you just said and belongs to writing. "Puisque" and "étant donné que" present the cause as already known and accepted by everyone. "À cause de" is negative, "grâce à" positive, "en raison de" strictly neutral and formal, and "faute de" means the cause is an absence.

examples.french: Les prix ont grimpé en raison de la pénurie d'énergie.
examples.english: Prices climbed owing to the energy shortage.
examples.note: neutral, formal register

examples.french: L'usine a fermé à cause d'une gestion désastreuse.
examples.english: The factory closed because of disastrous management.

examples.french: Grâce au plan de relance, l'emploi est reparti.
examples.english: Thanks to the stimulus plan, employment picked up again.

examples.french: Faute de liquidités, la société n'a pas pu payer ses salariés.
examples.english: For lack of cash, the company couldn't pay its employees.

examples.french: Puisque tout le monde le sait, autant le dire.
examples.english: Since everyone knows it, we may as well say it.

examples.french: La banque a chuté, car ses actifs ne valaient plus rien.
examples.english: The bank collapsed, for its assets were worth nothing any more.

blocks.tip: "Car" never starts a sentence in careful French; "parce que" can, but only when it answers a "pourquoi" question.

blocks.heading: Naming consequences
blocks.body: The mirror set is just as precise. "Donc" and "par conséquent" state a logical result, the second being much more formal. "Si bien que" and "de sorte que" describe a result that flowed naturally. "Au point que" adds intensity — so much so that. "D'où" + noun is a compact, very idiomatic way of concluding, and "c'est pourquoi" opens the concluding sentence of an argument.

examples.french: Les taux ont grimpé, si bien que les ménages ont cessé d'emprunter.
examples.english: Rates climbed, so that households stopped borrowing.

examples.french: Par conséquent, la consommation s'est effondrée.
examples.english: Consequently, consumption collapsed.

examples.french: La panique a gagné les marchés, au point que la Bourse a suspendu les échanges.
examples.english: Panic spread to the markets, to the point that the exchange suspended trading.

examples.french: Aucune visibilité, d'où la prudence des investisseurs.
examples.english: No visibility, hence investors' caution.
examples.note: d'où + noun, never + verb

examples.french: C'est pourquoi il faut agir maintenant.
examples.english: That is why we must act now.

examples.french: La crise a entraîné une vague de licenciements.
examples.english: The crisis brought about a wave of redundancies.

blocks.tip: "Du coup" means the same as "donc" but is strictly spoken French — never write it in a report or an exam essay.

blocks.heading: Cause: conjunction or preposition?
blocks.body: The single most common B2 mistake is mixing the two families. Conjunctions (parce que, puisque, étant donné que, car, comme) are followed by a CLAUSE with a conjugated verb. Prepositions (à cause de, grâce à, en raison de, faute de, du fait de) are followed by a NOUN or an infinitive. So: "en raison de la pénurie" but "parce qu'il y a une pénurie". "Comme" expressing cause must open the sentence.

examples.french: Comme la demande s'effondrait, l'usine a fermé.
examples.english: As demand was collapsing, the factory closed.
examples.note: "comme" always first in the sentence

examples.french: L'usine a fermé en raison de l'effondrement de la demande.
examples.english: The factory closed owing to the collapse in demand.

examples.french: Puisque vous connaissez le dossier, je serai bref.
examples.english: Since you know the file, I'll be brief.

examples.french: Faute d'avoir anticipé, ils ont tout perdu.
examples.english: For failing to anticipate, they lost everything.
examples.note: faute de + infinitif is possible

examples.french: Grâce à une trésorerie solide, elle a tenu.
examples.english: Thanks to solid cash reserves, she held on.

examples.french: Étant donné que les taux montent, on reporte l'achat.
examples.english: Given that rates are rising, we're postponing the purchase.

blocks.tip: "À cause de" always blames; using it for something positive ("à cause de son talent") sounds odd — use "grâce à".

blocks.heading: Consequence: indicative or subjunctive?
blocks.body: Consequence conjunctions normally take the INDICATIVE, because a result is a fact: "si bien que", "de sorte que" (result), "au point que", "tellement… que". The one trap is "de sorte que": with the SUBJUNCTIVE it stops meaning "so that" as a result and means "so that" as a PURPOSE. Compare: "Il a parlé lentement, de sorte que tout le monde a compris" (result, fact) and "Parlez lentement, de sorte que tout le monde comprenne" (aim).

examples.french: Les prix ont tellement grimpé que les gens ont arrêté d'acheter.
examples.english: Prices rose so much that people stopped buying.

examples.french: Il a agi vite, de sorte que la faillite a été évitée.
examples.english: He acted fast, so that bankruptcy was avoided.
examples.note: indicatif: a result that happened

examples.french: Simplifions le rapport, de sorte que chacun le comprenne.
examples.english: Let's simplify the report so that everyone understands it.
examples.note: subjonctif: an aim

examples.french: La dette a augmenté au point qu'elle dépasse le PIB.
examples.english: The debt rose to the point that it exceeds GDP.

examples.french: Il n'y a aucune visibilité, d'où le gel des embauches.
examples.english: There is no visibility, hence the hiring freeze.

examples.french: La confiance s'est effritée ; par conséquent, personne n'investit.
examples.english: Confidence crumbled; consequently, nobody is investing.

blocks.tip: In an exam essay, alternate: "par conséquent" and "c'est pourquoi" for formal writing, "si bien que" inside a sentence, and keep "du coup" for the café.

passages.title: Anatomie d'une crise
passages.french:
Toute crise commence par une histoire que tout le monde croit.
En 2006, cette histoire disait que le prix de l'immobilier américain ne pouvait pas baisser.
Étant donné que le bien prenait de la valeur chaque année, prêter à un ménage insolvable ne paraissait pas absurde : en cas de défaut, on revendait la maison plus cher.
Les banques ont donc prêté massivement, puis revendu ces créances à d'autres banques, si bien que plus personne ne savait qui portait le risque.
Quand les prix ont fini par reculer, le mécanisme s'est inversé au point que des établissements entiers se sont retrouvés insolvables en quelques jours.
La faillite de Lehman Brothers, en septembre 2008, a déclenché la panique.
En raison de la méfiance générale, les banques ont cessé de se prêter entre elles ; faute de crédit, les entreprises ont gelé leurs investissements ; par conséquent, les licenciements ont commencé.
Moins d'emplois, donc moins de revenus ; moins de revenus, donc moins de consommation : le cercle vicieux était enclenché.
L'État a fini par intervenir, non par générosité, mais parce que laisser tomber le système bancaire aurait coûté bien plus cher.
Dix ans plus tard, les économistes se disputent encore sur les causes.
Pour les uns, il s'agissait d'un accident conjoncturel, aggravé par la panique.
Pour les autres, le problème était structurel : une finance devenue trop grosse pour l'économie qu'elle était censée servir.
Ce qui est certain, c'est que la facture a été payée deux fois — d'abord par les contribuables, ensuite par les salariés soumis à dix ans d'austérité.
D'où la question qui revient à chaque nouvelle secousse : a-t-on vraiment retenu la leçon ?
passages.english:
Every crisis begins with a story that everyone believes.
In 2006, that story said that the price of American property could not fall.
Given that the asset gained value every year, lending to an insolvent household did not seem absurd: in case of default, you resold the house for more.
Banks therefore lent massively, then resold those debts to other banks, so that nobody knew any more who was carrying the risk.
When prices finally fell back, the mechanism went into reverse, to the point that entire institutions found themselves insolvent within days.
The bankruptcy of Lehman Brothers, in September 2008, triggered the panic.
Owing to the general distrust, banks stopped lending to each other; for lack of credit, companies froze their investments; consequently, the layoffs began.
Fewer jobs, therefore less income; less income, therefore less spending: the vicious circle was under way.
The state eventually stepped in, not out of generosity, but because letting the banking system fall would have cost far more.
Ten years later, economists are still arguing about the causes.
For some, it was a cyclical accident, made worse by panic.
For others, the problem was structural: a financial sector grown too big for the economy it was supposed to serve.
What is certain is that the bill was paid twice — first by taxpayers, then by employees subjected to ten years of austerity.
Hence the question that comes back with every new tremor: have we really learned the lesson?
